summary: Asks Path Computation Element working group drafts to include manageability sections, because manageability is too often added to protocols after the fact. It points to existing operations and management guidelines. Its status is historic.

eli5.summary: When building a toy, plan for how to fix it later. This asked authors of one group's documents to plan for running and watching their protocols.

questions: what is a manageability considerations section
what is a null manageability section
subtitle: A historic guide asking PCE working group drafts to say how their protocols will be operated and managed.

tldr.problem: Manageability is often bolted onto protocols after they are specified, standardized, implemented or deployed, which is sub-optimal.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends that every PCE Working Group Internet-Draft carry a Manageability Considerations section, with six recommended subsections, placed just before Security Considerations.
tldr.outcome: The PCE Working Group later adopted the general guidance in RFC 5706, so this document is no longer required and is kept as a Historic reference.

today: RFC 6123 is Historic. The PCE Working Group adopted the general guidance in RFC 5706, so this document is no longer required and is kept for historical reference.

sections.title: Why Manageability Needs Its Own Section
sections.content:
When new protocols or extensions are designed, not enough thought is often given to how they will be operated in the network. Problems are then understood only after implementation, sometimes after deployment, and retrofitting manageability is not always easy or architecturally pleasant.

RFC 6123 therefore recommended that every Internet-Draft in the PCE (Path Computation Element) Working Group include a Manageability Considerations section. The RFC admits that such a section does not guarantee a well-designed or manageable protocol, but it gives authors the chance to consider the issues. The document is not a protocol specification.
sections.eli5: If you only think about repairs after a toy is built, the repairs are awkward. Writing a repair plan first makes the toy easier to look after.

sections.title: What Manageability Means
sections.content:
Here manageability means the interactions between a network operator (a human or an application) and the network components, carried out to keep the network working correctly. These issues are often grouped under the acronym FCAPS: Fault management, Configuration, Accounting, Performance and Security.

Security is conventionally handled in a draft's own Security Considerations section, and the RFC does not reduce the need for that section. Authors should consider all aspects of FCAPS and how a protocol affects the operation of the whole network.

The RFC also separates the management plane (management messages between management applications and network nodes) from the control plane (signaling and routing) and the forwarding plane (user traffic).
sections.eli5: Looking after a network is like looking after a school: you handle problems, settings, record keeping, speed and safety. The management plane is the office, separate from the classrooms where the real work happens.

sections.title: Presence and Placement of the Section
sections.content:
A draft SHOULD contain a Manageability Considerations section even when it has no manageability requirements. This null section shows the reader that manageability was considered. It SHOULD NOT consist only of the statement that there are no new requirements; it SHOULD briefly explain why, summarizing the mechanisms that already exist.

A non-null section SHOULD contain at least these subsections: Control of Function through Configuration and Policy; Information and Data Models, e.g., MIB modules; Liveness Detection and Monitoring; Verifying Correct Operation; Requirements on Other Protocols and Functional Components; and Impact on Network Operation. An irrelevant subsection SHOULD still appear, with a statement saying why it is not relevant.

Authors can and SHOULD add other subsections as needed. The whole section SHOULD be placed immediately before the Security Considerations section.
sections.eli5: Even if there is nothing to fix, you still write a note saying why. Then everyone knows you thought about it instead of forgetting.

sections.title: Guidance for Each Subsection
sections.content:
Configuration and policy: identify the elements an operator can control, such as timers, and which elements may be subject to policy. A reference to another section is enough if the full description is elsewhere.

Information and data models: describe the models needed, including any MIB modules. Giving high-level object groupings and the major manageable entities is helpful. The RFC notes that MIB modules may be decreasing in significance, and lists options such as the SNMP-based MIB model and the NETCONF model.

Liveness and monitoring: highlight how faults in the control plane and data plane are detected and what management actions are expected when one is found. Verifying correct operation: explain how correct operation can be tested, end to end and per network element.

Other protocols and impact: say what the new protocol requires of other protocols and components, and outline its effect on existing networks, including scaling. Backward compatibility is called very important: whether all nodes must be upgraded, whether versions can run side by side, and whether a maintenance period is needed. Anything else needed to understand manageability goes in an additional section.
sections.eli5: Each part of the note answers a simple question. What can be adjusted? Is it still alive? Is it working right? What else does it need? What happens to the old stuff when the new thing arrives?

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security concerns and makes no request to IANA. Drafts SHOULD NOT introduce new codepoints, name spaces or IANA requests within the Manageability Considerations section.

There is, however, an overlap between security and management. Manageability aspects of security SHOULD be covered in each draft's Security Considerations, and any new security considerations introduced by the manageability section MUST be covered there. The RFC argues that designing manageability up front gives a more robust protocol, whereas retrofitting it can make a protocol more vulnerable, including through the new management facilities.
sections.eli5: Adding a back door to fix things later can let the wrong people in. Planning the repair door from the start lets you lock it properly.
